title: On-Prem First Responder Checklist + Troubleshooting Lab Notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact "first-responder" playbook and lab-note dump for on-prem / VPC private deployments. It is deliberately prescriptive: immediate triage steps, reproducible lab tests, Terraform module sanity checks, and a safe upgrade/canary checklist. Keep this on your laptop for paged incidents and as a base for runbook cut-and-paste.

Audience and scope:
- Eng SREs and private-deploy engineers handling initial install failures, runtime crashes, and upgrade regressions.
- Focused on common failure classes we see in private installs: network path/mTLS issues, TF state drift, bootstrap timingouts, container runtime unit failures, GPU driver conflicts, and KV/cache mismatches that lead to model-serving errors.

Quick triage one-liner (what to run first):
1) Check cluster nodes: kubectl get nodes -o wide 
2) Inspect systemd and runtime units on failing host: journalctl -u redwood-runtime.service -n 400 --no-pager
3) Validate control-plane health: curl -sS http://localhost:8080/healthz || curl -sS https://127.0.0.1:8443/healthz -k
4) Confirm TF state sanity: terraform state list | head -n 30 (from infrastructure repo tag used during install)

First-responder checklist (ordered, actionable):
- Safety + scope: who is on-call, which customer cluster (id), which model/version is pinned, affected routes. Put the incident in #private-deployments and create PRIV-<cluster>-<shortid>.
- High-level status: control-plane (api/console), serving runtime (redwood-runtime), infra (kube/node, storage), network (VPC peers, firewall), upgrade activity (was an upgrade running?).
- JVM/Runtime / GPU check: nvidia-smi || lsmod | grep nvidia; check driver mismatch errors in dmesg, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log.
- Storage sanity: df -h and ls -la /var/lib/redwood/cache; check for out-of-space or inode exhaustion.
- Health endpoints: curl /healthz on each control-plane pod, and curl /v1/serve/ready for runtime.
- Recent changes: git commit hash of terraform modules and helm charts used; note drift from live cluster.

Common failure signatures and immediate remedies:
1) Bootstrap never completes (init stuck at "waiting for seeds")
   Symptoms: terraform apply completed, but runtime nodes show long provisioning, pods CrashLoopBackOff, bootstrap logs show repeated leader-election timeouts.
   Fast checks: tail -n 200 bootstrap logs on installer node, check /etc/hosts entries for control-plane VIP, DNS resolution: dig @<customer-dns> api.<cluster>
   Likely causes: time skew across nodes, broken CA trust (mTLS), firewall blocking port 2380/2379 (etcd), kubelet not registered due to token mismatch.
   Quick fixes: ensure NTP, re-run token join script from control-plane and capture output, if CA mismatch regenerate ephemeral CA only after escalation.

2) Runtime service failing with KV cache errors ("KV mismatch: seq=... not found")
   Symptoms: model load failures, repeated full-evictions, higher token latency and stale responses.
   Fast checks: cat /var/log/redwood/runtime.log | grep -i "kv" -n | tail -n 80
   Hypothesis: cache persisted from older runtime version -> incompatible layout.
   Fix approach: stop runtime, move cache dir (/var/lib/redwood/cache -> /var/lib/redwood/cache.bak.<ts>), restart and verify warm-up. If rollback required, restore cache. Add migration path in tf module or runtime init script.

3) Serving latency spikes after upgrade (p95 >> baseline)
   Symptoms: tokens/sec drop, queue saturating, request timeouts at proxy.
   Checks: runtime /proc/softirqs, top, nvidia-smi, check kernel dmesg for GPU OOMs, examine per-route batching metrics in console.
   Mitigation: enable degraded fallback (route to smaller model variant), temporarily reduce batch target size, scale out pods if Dedicated capacity in config.

4) Terraform apply fails with "local-exec script exit 2" or state lock timeouts
   Symptoms: partial infra created, missing resources in state, subsequent applies failing.
   Checks: terraform init & providers versions, terraform version used by installer, check remote state backend connectivity (S3/GCS/Consul).
   Remediation: rescue state with terraform state pull > state.json, then terraform state rm for orphaned resources, re-run apply. If locking issue, identify lock holder via backend console and force-unlock after confirming.

Repro lab harness (how to simulate common errors quickly):
- Broken CA/mTLS: run l3 network namespace separating certs between control-plane and node, simulate blocked port 2380 using iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 2380 -j REJECT, then attempt join.
- Cache layout drift: start a runtime with old cache dir from earlier release and run unit tests that call runtime's cache-open path.
- Disk pressure: create a loopback file system limited to 2GB and bind-mount as /var/lib/redwood to reproduce writes failing.

Terraform module notes (short, for immediate checks):
- Always record the module tag/commit used during install in /opt/redwood/install-info.json (module_commit, installer_version, tf_version).
- Common drift sources: manual edits to K8s resources, external autoscalers, and node labels changed for GPU types. Use terraform state list | grep redwood_ to find resources we own.
- Debugging provider errors: enable TF_LOG=DEBUG when running apply in lab to capture provider stacktrace; export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR for provider caching.
- Roll-forward safety: keep a small "bootstrap" var in modules that gates replacing critical resources (etcd/discovery). For upgrades, set bootstrap=false after green verification.

Upgrade/canary checklist (safe cadence):
- Pre-upgrade: record metrics snapshot (p50/p95 latency, model throughput, token cost) + backing up terraform remote state snapshot + kube-resources: kubectl get all --all-namespaces -o yaml > pre-upgrade-<ts>.yaml.
- Stage upgrade to non-prod replica if available. If not: canary on single node using node_affinity and draining technique.
- Post-upgrade smoke tests (automated): health endpoints, short end-to-end generation with pinned prompt set, model load/unload loops, small-load closed-loop test (iperf3 for network, grpc ping if enabled).
- Observability: configure temporary increased retention of traces for upgrade window and create regression alert for >2x p95.
- Rollback plan: have the exact terraform/helm commit to revert to and a documented manual rollback step: drain, replace image tag, restart runtime, re-check cache migration.

Quick commands (copy-paste):
- node summary: kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NODE:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.conditions[-1].type,AGE:.metadata.creationTimestamp
- pod logs (follow last 400 lines): kubectl logs -n redwood <runtime-pod> -c runtime --tail=400 -f
- check journalds: ssh root@host sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime.service --since "2 hours ago" | tail -n 200
- terraform rescue: terraform state pull > /tmp/state.json && terraform state list | sed -n '1,60p'
- test health: for HOST in $(kubectl get pods -n redwood -l app=runtime -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'); do curl -sS http://$HOST:8080/healthz || echo "$HOST fail"; done

Escalation matrix and what to include in PagerDuty message:
- On-call private-deploy -> SRE lead -> Runtime eng on-call -> infra/team that owns host's hypervisor.
- Include: cluster id, affected model or endpoint, last successful commit hash, captain's screenshot of metrics (p95/p50), core logs (last 200 lines) and TF state diff snippet if relevant.

Hypothesis matrix (helpful during post-mortem):
- Column fields we use in incident docs: symptom, trivial test to run, probability (low/med/high), required rollback (yes/no), follow-up action.
- Example row: "model loads fail" / "curl /v1/models returns 503" / high / manual restart runtime / add migration guard for cache layout.

Retention and follow-up actions (post-incident):
- Create a short retro: what was fixed, what changes to TF modules or runtime init scripts to avoid reoccurrence, and whether to add an automated alert or runbook step.
- If cache migration issues caused outage, schedule a small upgrade of the runtime with a migration path and add tests to CI that exercise cache compatibility.

Appendix: common log snippets and what they usually mean
- "etcd: failed to commit entry" -> often disk IO or corrupted DB, check etcd volume and iops, and whether compaction ran concurrently.
- "TLS: unknown certificate" -> CA mismatch or missing intermediate chain; verify cert fingerprints across nodes.
- "kv-eviction: unexpected key format" -> runtime binary and cache layout mismatch; treat as migration bug.

Notes / TODOs for next revision:
- Add small python script to gather all pre-upgrade artifacts and upload to S3 for faster incident repro.
- Add exact TF module import commands we used to rescue state previously.
- Convert the lab harness into a k3s-based testkit for quickly reproducing common failure modes in CI.

If you copy this into an incident channel, replace sensitive fields (customer ips, s3 buckets, private keys) and keep only the hashes and references. This doc is intentionally terse and action-first; expand any section into a stable runbook once the triage pattern proves repeatable.

End of doc.
